functions.name: addProp
functions.summary:
Add a new property to an object.

The function doesn't do any checks on the input object. If the property
already exists it will be overwritten, and the type of the new value is not
checked against the previous type.

Use [`set`](#set) to override values explicitly with better protections.

signatures.exampleHtml: addProp({ firstName: 'john' }, 'lastName', 'doe'); // => {firstName: 'john', lastName: 'doe'}
addProp('lastName', 'doe')({ firstName: 'john' }); // => {firstName: 'john', lastName: 'doe'}

functions.name: clone
functions.summary:
Creates a deep copy of the value. Supported types: [plain objects](#isPlainObject),
`Array`, `number`, `string`, `boolean`, `Date`, and `RegExp`. Functions are
assigned by reference rather than copied. Class instances or any other
built-in type that isn't mentioned above are not supported (but might
work).

signatures.exampleHtml: clone({ foo: 'bar' }); // {foo: 'bar'}
pipe({ foo: 'bar' }, clone()); // {foo: 'bar'}

functions.name: entries
functions.summary: Returns an array of key/values of the enumerable properties of an object.

signatures.exampleHtml: entries({ a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }); // => [['a', 1], ['b', 2], ['c', 3]]

params.name: data
params.description: Object to return keys and values of.

signatures.exampleHtml: pipe({ a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }, entries()); // => [['a', 1], ['b', 2], ['c', 3]]

functions.name: evolve
functions.summary:
Creates a new object by applying functions that is included in `evolver` object parameter
to the `data` object parameter according to their corresponding path.

Functions included in `evolver` object will not be invoked
if its corresponding key does not exist in the `data` object.
Also, values included in `data` object will be kept as is
if its corresponding key does not exist in the `evolver` object.

signatures.exampleHtml: const evolver = { count: add(1), time: { elapsed: add(1), remaining: add(-1) }, }; const data = { id: 10, count: 10, time: { elapsed: 100, remaining: 1400 }, }; evolve(data, evolver); // => { // id: 10, // count: 11, // time: { elapsed: 101, remaining: 1399 }, // }

params.name: object
params.description:
Object whose value is applied to the corresponding function
that is defined in `evolver` at the same path.

params.name: evolver
params.description:
Object that include functions that is applied to
the corresponding value of `data` object at the same path.

signatures.exampleHtml: const evolver = { count: add(1), time: { elapsed: add(1), remaining: add(-1) }, }; const data = { id: 10, count: 10, time: { elapsed: 100, remaining: 1400 }, }; pipe(data, evolve(evolver)); // => { // id: 10, // count: 11, // time: { elapsed: 101, remaining: 1399 }, // }

params.name: evolver
params.description:
Object that include functions that is applied to
the corresponding value of `data` object at the same path.

functions.name: forEachObj
functions.summary:
Iterate an object using a defined callback function.

The dataLast version returns the original object (instead of not returning
anything (`void`)) to allow using it in a pipe. The returned object is the
same reference as the input object, and not a shallow copy of it!

signatures.exampleHtml: forEachObj({ a: 1 }, (val, key, obj) => { console.log(`${key}: ${val}`); }); // "a: 1"

params.name: data
params.description: The object who'se entries would be iterated on.

params.name: callbackfn
params.description: A function to execute for each element in the array.

signatures.exampleHtml: pipe( { a: 1 }, forEachObj((val, key) => console.log(`${key}: ${val}`)), ); // "a: 1"

params.name: callbackfn
params.description: A function to execute for each element in the array.

returns.description: The original object (the ref itself, not a shallow copy of it).

functions.name: fromEntries
functions.summary:
Creates a new object from an array of tuples by pairing up first and second elements as {[key]: value}.
If a tuple is not supplied for any element in the array, the element will be ignored
If duplicate keys exist, the tuple with the greatest index in the input array will be preferred.

The strict option supports more sophisticated use-cases like those that would
result when calling the strict `toPairs` function.

There are several other functions that could be used to build an object from
an array:
[`fromKeys`](#fromKeys) - Builds an object from an array of *keys* and a mapper for values.
[`indexBy`](#indexBy) - Builds an object from an array of *values* and a mapper for keys.
[`pullObject`](#pullObject) - Builds an object from an array of items with mappers for *both* keys and values.
Refer to the docs for more details.

signatures.exampleHtml: fromEntries([ ['a', 'b'], ['c', 'd'], ]); // => {a: 'b', c: 'd'}
pipe( [ ['a', 'b'], ['c', 'd'], ] as const, fromEntries(), ); // => {a: 'b', c: 'd'}

functions.name: fromKeys
functions.summary:
Creates an object that maps each key in `data` to the result of `mapper` for
that key. Duplicate keys are overwritten, guaranteeing that `mapper` is run
for each item in `data`.

There are several other functions that could be used to build an object from
an array:
[`indexBy`](#indexBy) - Builds an object from an array of *values* and a mapper for keys.
[`pullObject`](#pullObject) - Builds an object from an array of items with mappers for *both* keys and values.
[`fromEntries`](#fromEntries) - Builds an object from an array of key-value pairs.
Refer to the docs for more details.

signatures.example:
fromKeys(['cat', 'dog'], length()); // { cat: 3, dog: 3 } (typed as Partial<Record<"cat" | "dog", number>>)
fromKeys([1, 2], add(1)); // { 1: 2, 2: 3 } (typed as Partial<Record<1 | 2, number>>)
signatures.exampleHtml: fromKeys(['cat', 'dog'], length()); // { cat: 3, dog: 3 } (typed as Partial<Record<"cat" | "dog", number>>) fromKeys([1, 2], add(1)); // { 1: 2, 2: 3 } (typed as Partial<Record<1 | 2, number>>)

params.name: data
params.description:
An array of keys of the output object. All items in the array
would be keys in the output array.

params.name: mapper
params.description:
Takes a key and returns the value that would be associated
with that key.

signatures.example:
pipe(['cat', 'dog'], fromKeys(length())); // { cat: 3, dog: 3 } (typed as Partial<Record<"cat" | "dog", number>>)
pipe([1, 2], fromKeys(add(1))); // { 1: 2, 2: 3 } (typed as Partial<Record<1 | 2, number>>)
signatures.exampleHtml: pipe(['cat', 'dog'], fromKeys(length())); // { cat: 3, dog: 3 } (typed as Partial<Record<"cat" | "dog", number>>) pipe([1, 2], fromKeys(add(1))); // { 1: 2, 2: 3 } (typed as Partial<Record<1 | 2, number>>)

params.name: mapper
params.description:
Takes a key and returns the value that would be associated
with that key.

functions.name: invert
functions.summary:
Returns an object whose keys and values are swapped. If the object contains duplicate values,
subsequent values will overwrite previous values.

signatures.exampleHtml: invert({ a: 'd', b: 'e', c: 'f' }); // => { d: "a", e: "b", f: "c" }
pipe({ a: 'd', b: 'e', c: 'f' }, invert()); // => { d: "a", e: "b", f: "c" }

functions.name: keys
functions.summary: Returns a new array containing the keys of the array or object.

signatures.exampleHtml: keys(['x', 'y', 'z']); // => ['0', '1', '2'] keys({ a: 'x', b: 'y', 5: 'z' }); // => ['a', 'b', '5']

params.name: data
params.description: Either an array or an object.

signatures.exampleHtml: pipe(['x', 'y', 'z'], keys()); // => ['0', '1', '2'] pipe({ a: 'x', b: 'y', 5: 'z' } as const, keys()); // => ['a', 'b', '5']

functions.name: mapKeys
functions.summary: Maps keys of `object` and keeps the same values.

signatures.example: mapKeys({ a: 1, b: 2 }, (key, value) => key + value); // => { a1: 1, b2: 2 }
signatures.exampleHtml: mapKeys({ a: 1, b: 2 }, (key, value) => key + value); // => { a1: 1, b2: 2 }
pipe( { a: 1, b: 2 }, mapKeys((key, value) => key + value), ); // => { a1: 1, b2: 2 }

functions.name: mapValues
functions.summary:
Maps values of `object` and keeps the same keys. Symbol keys are not passed
to the mapper and will be removed from the output object.

To also copy the symbol keys to the output use merge:
`merge(data, mapValues(data, mapper))`).

signatures.example: mapValues({ a: 1, b: 2 }, (value, key) => value + key); // => {a: '1a', b: '2b'}
signatures.exampleHtml: mapValues({ a: 1, b: 2 }, (value, key) => value + key); // => {a: '1a', b: '2b'}
pipe( { a: 1, b: 2 }, mapValues((value, key) => value + key), ); // => {a: '1a', b: '2b'}

functions.name: merge
functions.summary:
Merges two objects into one by combining their properties, effectively
creating a new object that incorporates elements from both. The merge
operation prioritizes the second object's properties, allowing them to
overwrite those from the first object with the same names.

Equivalent to `{ ...data, ...source }`.

signatures.exampleHtml: merge({ x: 1, y: 2 }, { y: 10, z: 2 }); // => { x: 1, y: 10, z: 2 }

params.name: data
params.description:
The destination object, serving as the basis for the merge.
Properties from this object are included in the new object, but will be
overwritten by properties from the source object with matching keys.

params.name: source
params.description:
The source object, whose properties will be included in the
new object. If properties in this object share keys with properties in the
destination object, the values from the source object will be used in the
new object.

returns.description:
An object fully containing `source`, and any properties from `data`
that don't share a name with any property in `source`.

signatures.exampleHtml: pipe({ x: 1, y: 2 }, merge({ y: 10, z: 2 })); // => { x: 1, y: 10, z: 2 }

params.name: source
params.description:
The source object, whose properties will be included in the
new object. If properties in this object share keys with properties in the
destination object, the values from the source object will be used in the
new object.

returns.description:
An object fully containing `source`, and any properties from `data`
that don't share a name with any property in `source`.

functions.name: mergeDeep
functions.summary: Merges the `source` object into the `destination` object. The merge is similar to performing `{ ...destination, ... source }` (where disjoint values from each object would be copied as-is, and for any overlapping props the value from `source` would be used); But for *each prop* (`p`), if **both** `destination` and `source` have a **plain-object** as a value, the value would be taken as the result of recursively deepMerging them (`result.p === deepMerge(destination.p, source.p)`).

signatures.example: mergeDeep({ foo: 'bar', x: 1 }, { foo: 'baz', y: 2 }); // => { foo: 'baz', x: 1, y: 2 }
signatures.exampleHtml: mergeDeep({ foo: 'bar', x: 1 }, { foo: 'baz', y: 2 }); // => { foo: 'baz', x: 1, y: 2 }

params.name: destination
params.description: The object to merge into. In general, this object would have it's values overridden.

params.name: source
params.description: The object to merge from. In general, shared keys would be taken from this object.

returns.description: The merged object.

signatures.example: pipe({ foo: 'bar', x: 1 }, mergeDeep({ foo: 'baz', y: 2 })); // => { foo: 'baz', x: 1, y: 2 }
signatures.exampleHtml: pipe({ foo: 'bar', x: 1 }, mergeDeep({ foo: 'baz', y: 2 })); // => { foo: 'baz', x: 1, y: 2 }

params.name: source
params.description: The object to merge from. In general, shared keys would be taken from this object.

returns.description: The merged object.

functions.name: objOf
functions.summary: Creates an object containing a single `key:value` pair.

signatures.exampleHtml: objOf(10, 'a'); // => { a: 10 }
pipe(10, objOf('a')); // => { a: 10 }

functions.name: omit
functions.summary: Returns a partial copy of an object omitting the keys specified.

signatures.exampleHtml: omit({ a: 1, b: 2, c: 3, d: 4 }, ['a', 'd']); // => { b: 2, c: 3 }
pipe({ a: 1, b: 2, c: 3, d: 4 }, omit(['a', 'd'])); // => { b: 2, c: 3 }

functions.name: omitBy
functions.summary:
Creates a shallow copy of the data, and then removes any keys that the
predicate rejects. Symbol keys are not passed to the predicate and would be
passed through to the output as-is.

See [`pickBy`](#pickBy) for a complementary function which starts with an empty object
and adds the entries that the predicate accepts. Because it is additive,
symbol keys will not be passed through to the output object.

signatures.example: omitBy({ a: 1, b: 2, A: 3, B: 4 }, (val, key) => key.toUpperCase() === key); // => {a: 1, b: 2}
signatures.exampleHtml: omitBy({ a: 1, b: 2, A: 3, B: 4 }, (val, key) => key.toUpperCase() === key); // => {a: 1, b: 2}

params.name: predicate
params.description:
A function that takes the value, key, and the data itself
and returns `true` if the entry shouldn't be part of the output object, or
`false` to keep it. If the function is a type-guard on the value the output
type would be narrowed accordingly.

returns.description:
A shallow copy of the input object with the rejected entries
removed.

signatures.example: omitBy((val, key) => key.toUpperCase() === key)({ a: 1, b: 2, A: 3, B: 4 }); // => {a: 1, b: 2}
signatures.exampleHtml: omitBy((val, key) => key.toUpperCase() === key)({ a: 1, b: 2, A: 3, B: 4 }); // => {a: 1, b: 2}

functions.name: pathOr
functions.summary:
Gets the value at `path` of `object`. If the resolved value is `null` or `undefined`, the `defaultValue` is returned in its place.

**DEPRECATED**: Use `defaultTo(prop(object, ...path), defaultValue)`
instead!

signatures.exampleHtml: pathOr({ x: 10 }, ['y'], 2); // 2 pathOr({ y: 10 }, ['y'], 2); // 10

params.name: path
params.description: The path of the property to get.

signatures.exampleHtml: pipe({ x: 10 }, pathOr(['y'], 2)); // 2 pipe({ y: 10 }, pathOr(['y'], 2)); // 10

params.name: path
params.description: The path of the property to get.

functions.name: pick
functions.summary: Creates an object composed of the picked `data` properties.

signatures.exampleHtml: pick({ a: 1, b: 2, c: 3, d: 4 }, ['a', 'd']); // => { a: 1, d: 4 }
pipe({ a: 1, b: 2, c: 3, d: 4 }, pick(['a', 'd'])); // => { a: 1, d: 4 }

functions.name: pickBy
functions.summary:
Iterates over the entries of `data` and reconstructs the object using only
entries that `predicate` accepts. Symbol keys are not passed to the predicate
and would be filtered out from the output object.

See [`omitBy`](#omitBy) for a complementary function which starts with a shallow copy of
the input object and removes the entries that the predicate rejects. Because
it is subtractive symbol keys would be copied over to the output object.
See also [`entries`](#entries), [`filter`](#filter), and [`fromEntries`](#fromEntries) which could be used to build
your own version of [`pickBy`](#pickBy) if you need more control (though the resulting
type might be less precise).

signatures.example: pickBy({ a: 1, b: 2, A: 3, B: 4 }, (val, key) => key.toUpperCase() === key); // => {A: 3, B: 4}
signatures.exampleHtml: pickBy({ a: 1, b: 2, A: 3, B: 4 }, (val, key) => key.toUpperCase() === key); // => {A: 3, B: 4}

params.name: predicate
params.description:
A function that takes the value, key, and the data itself
and returns true if the entry should be part of the output object, or `false`
to remove it. If the function is a type-guard on the value the output type
would be narrowed accordingly.

returns.description:
A shallow copy of the input object with the rejected entries
removed.

signatures.exampleHtml: pipe( { a: 1, b: 2, A: 3, B: 4 }, pickBy((val, key) => key.toUpperCase() === key), ); // => {A: 3, B: 4}

params.name: predicate
params.description:
A function that takes the value, key, and the data itself
and returns true if the entry should be part of the output object, or `false`
to remove it. If the function is a type-guard on the value the output type
would be narrowed accordingly.

functions.name: prop
functions.summary:
Gets the value of the given property from an object. Nested properties can
be accessed by providing a variadic array of keys that define the path from
the root to the desired property. Arrays can be accessed by using numeric
keys. Unions and optional properties are handled gracefully by returning
`undefined` early for any non-existing property on the path. Paths are
validated against the object type to provide stronger type safety, better
compile-time errors, and to enable autocompletion in IDEs.

To check whether a key exists on the object, use [`hasProp`](#hasProp).

signatures.exampleHtml: prop({ foo: { bar: 'baz' } }, 'foo'); //=> { bar: 'baz' } prop({ foo: { bar: 'baz' } }, 'foo', 'bar'); //=> 'baz' prop(['cat', 'dog'], 1); //=> 'dog'

params.name: data
params.description: The object or array to access.

params.name: key
params.description: The key(s) for the property to extract.

signatures.exampleHtml: pipe({ foo: { bar: 'baz' } }, prop('foo')); //=> { bar: 'baz' } pipe({ foo: { bar: 'baz' } }, prop('foo', 'bar')); //=> 'baz' pipe(['cat', 'dog'], prop(1)); //=> 'dog'

params.name: key
params.description: The key(s) for the property to extract.

functions.name: pullObject
functions.summary:
Creates an object that maps the result of `valueExtractor` with a key
resulting from running `keyExtractor` on each item in `data`. Duplicate keys
are overwritten, guaranteeing that the extractor functions are run on each
item in `data`.

There are several other functions that could be used to build an object from
an array:
[`fromKeys`](#fromKeys) - Builds an object from an array of *keys* and a mapper for values.
[`indexBy`](#indexBy) - Builds an object from an array of *values* and a mapper for keys.
[`fromEntries`](#fromEntries) - Builds an object from an array of key-value pairs.
Refer to the docs for more details.

signatures.exampleHtml: pullObject( [ { name: 'john', email: 'john@perkakas.com' }, { name: 'jane', email: 'jane@perkakas.com' }, ], prop('name'), prop('email'), ); // => { john: "john@perkakas.com", jane: "jane@perkakas.com" }

params.name: data
params.description: The items used to pull/extract the keys and values from.

params.name: valueExtractor
params.description: Computes the value for the item.

signatures.exampleHtml: pipe( [ { name: 'john', email: 'john@perkakas.com' }, { name: 'jane', email: 'jane@perkakas.com' }, ], pullObject(prop('name'), prop('email')), ); // => { john: "john@perkakas.com", jane: "jane@perkakas.com" }

params.name: valueExtractor
params.description: Computes the value for the item.

functions.name: set
functions.summary:
Sets the `value` at [`prop`](#prop) of `object`.

To add a new property to an object, or to override its type, use [`addProp`](#addProp)
instead, and to set a property within a nested object use [`setPath`](#setPath).

signatures.exampleHtml: set({ a: 1 }, 'a', 2); // => { a: 2 }
pipe({ a: 1 }, set('a', 2)); // => { a: 2 }

functions.name: setPath
functions.summary:
Sets the value at `path` of `object`.

For simple cases where the path is only one level deep, prefer [`set`](#set) instead.

signatures.exampleHtml: setPath({ a: { b: 1 } }, ['a', 'b'], 2); // => { a: { b: 2 } }
pipe({ a: { b: 1 } }, setPath(['a', 'b'], 2)); // { a: { b: 2 } }

functions.name: swapProps
functions.summary: Swaps the values of two properties in an object based on the provided keys.

signatures.exampleHtml: swapProps({ a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }, 'a', 'b'); // => {a: 2, b: 1, c: 3}

returns.description: Returns the manipulated object.

signatures.exampleHtml: swapProps('a', 'b')({ a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }); // => {a: 2, b: 1, c: 3}

returns.description: Returns the manipulated object.

functions.name: values
functions.summary: Returns a new array containing the values of the array or object.

signatures.exampleHtml: values(['x', 'y', 'z']); // => ['x', 'y', 'z'] values({ a: 'x', b: 'y', c: 'z' }); // => ['x', 'y', 'z']

params.name: data
params.description: Either an array or an object.

signatures.exampleHtml: pipe(['x', 'y', 'z'], values()); // => ['x', 'y', 'z'] pipe({ a: 'x', b: 'y', c: 'z' }, values()); // => ['x', 'y', 'z'] pipe({ a: 'x', b: 'y', c: 'z' }, values(), first()); // => 'x'

functions.name: capitalize
functions.summary:
Makes the first character of a string uppercase while leaving the rest
unchanged.

It uses the built-in [`String.prototype.toUpperCase`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/toUpperCase)
for the runtime and the built-in [`Capitalize`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/template-literal-types.html#capitalizestringtype)
utility type for typing and thus shares their _[locale inaccuracies](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/toLocaleUpperCase#description)_.

For display purposes, prefer using the CSS pseudo-element [`::first-letter`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/::first-letter) to target
just the first letter of the word, and [`text-transform: uppercase`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/text-transform#uppercase)
to capitalize it. This transformation **is** locale-aware.

For other case manipulations see: [`toUpperCase`](#toUpperCase), [`toLowerCase`](#toLowerCase),
[`uncapitalize`](#uncapitalize), [`toCamelCase`](#toCamelCase), [`toKebabCase`](#toKebabCase), [`toSnakeCase`](#toSnakeCase), and
[`toTitleCase`](#toTitleCase).

signatures.exampleHtml: capitalize('hello world'); // "Hello world"
pipe('hello world', capitalize()); // "Hello world"

functions.name: endsWith
functions.summary:
Determines whether a string ends with the provided suffix, and refines the
output type if possible.

This function is a wrapper around the built-in [`String.prototype.endsWith`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/endsWith)
method, but doesn't expose the `endPosition` parameter. To check only up to a
specific position, use `endsWith(sliceString(data, 0, endPosition), suffix)`.

signatures.example:
endsWith('hello world', 'world'); //=> true
endsWith('hello world' as string, 'hello'); //=> false
signatures.exampleHtml: endsWith('hello world', 'world'); //=> true endsWith('hello world' as string, 'hello'); //=> false

params.name: suffix
params.description: The string to check for at the end.

signatures.example:
pipe('hello world', endsWith('world')); //=> true
pipe('hello world', endsWith('hello')); //=> false
signatures.exampleHtml: pipe('hello world', endsWith('world')); //=> true pipe('hello world', endsWith('hello')); //=> false

params.name: suffix
params.description: The string to check for at the end.

functions.name: humanReadableFileSize
functions.summary: Returns human readable file size.

signatures.exampleHtml: humanReadableFileSize(1000); // => '1.0 kB' humanReadableFileSize(2097152, 1024); // => '2.0 Mib'

functions.name: randomString
functions.summary:
A [pseudo-random](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_number_generator) [alpha-numeric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphanumericals)
[string](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String).

It is not [cryptographically secure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptographically_secure_pseudorandom_number_generator)!

signatures.exampleHtml: randomString(5); // => aB92J

params.name: length
params.description: The length of the random string.

returns.description: The random string.

signatures.exampleHtml: pipe(5, randomString()); // => aB92J

returns.description: The random string.

functions.name: sliceString
functions.summary:
Extracts a section of a string between two indices.

This function is a wrapper around the built-in [`String.prototype.slice`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/slice)
method.

signatures.exampleHtml: sliceString('abcdefghijkl', 1); // => `bcdefghijkl` sliceString('abcdefghijkl', 4, 7); // => `efg`

params.name: indexStart
params.description:
The index of the first character to include in the
returned substring.

params.name: indexEnd
params.description:
The index of the first character to exclude from the
returned substring.

returns.description: A new string containing the extracted section of the string.

signatures.exampleHtml: sliceString(1)('abcdefghijkl'); // => `bcdefghijkl` sliceString(4, 7)('abcdefghijkl'); // => `efg`

params.name: indexStart
params.description:
The index of the first character to include in the
returned substring.

params.name: indexEnd
params.description:
The index of the first character to exclude from the
returned substring, or `undefined` for the rest of the string.

returns.description: A new string containing the extracted section of the string.

functions.name: slugify
functions.summary: Turn any string into a URL/DOM safe string.

signatures.exampleHtml: slugify('FooBar'); // => 'foobar' slugify('This!-is*&%#@^up!'); // => 'this-is-up'

functions.name: split
functions.summary:
Splits a string into an array of substrings using a separator pattern.

This function is a wrapper around the built-in [`String.prototype.split`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/split)
method.

signatures.exampleHtml: split('a,b,c', ','); //=> ["a", "b", "c"] split('a,b,c', ',', 2); //=> ["a", "b"] split('a1b2c3d', /\d/u); //=> ["a", "b", "c", "d"]

params.name: separator
params.description:
The pattern describing where each split should occur. Can
be a string, or a regular expression.

params.name: limit
params.description:
A non-negative integer specifying a limit on the number of
substrings to be included in the array. If provided, splits the string at
each occurrence of the specified separator, but stops when limit entries have
been placed in the array. Any leftover text is not included in the array at
all. The array may contain fewer entries than limit if the end of the string
is reached before the limit is reached. If limit is 0, [] is returned.

returns.description:
An array of strings, split at each point where the separator occurs
in the given string.

signatures.exampleHtml: pipe('a,b,c', split(',')); //=> ["a", "b", "c"] pipe('a,b,c', split(',', 2)); //=> ["a", "b"] pipe('a1b2c3d', split(/\d/u)); //=> ["a", "b", "c", "d"]

params.name: separator
params.description:
The pattern describing where each split should occur. Can
be a string, or a regular expression.

params.name: limit
params.description:
A non-negative integer specifying a limit on the number of
substrings to be included in the array. If provided, splits the string at
each occurrence of the specified separator, but stops when limit entries have
been placed in the array. Any leftover text is not included in the array at
all. The array may contain fewer entries than limit if the end of the string
is reached before the limit is reached. If limit is 0, [] is returned.

returns.description:
An array of strings, split at each point where the separator occurs
in the given string.

functions.name: startsWith
functions.summary:
Determines whether a string begins with the provided prefix, and refines the
output type if possible.

This function is a wrapper around the built-in [`String.prototype.startsWith`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/startsWith)
method, but doesn't expose the `position` parameter. To check from a specific
position, use `startsWith(sliceString(data, position), prefix)`.

signatures.example:
startsWith('hello world', 'hello'); //=> true
startsWith('hello world' as string, 'world'); //=> false
signatures.exampleHtml: startsWith('hello world', 'hello'); //=> true startsWith('hello world' as string, 'world'); //=> false

params.name: prefix
params.description: The string to check for at the beginning.

signatures.example:
pipe('hello world', startsWith('hello')); //=> true
pipe('hello world', startsWith('world')); //=> false
signatures.exampleHtml: pipe('hello world', startsWith('hello')); //=> true pipe('hello world', startsWith('world')); //=> false

params.name: prefix
params.description: The string to check for at the beginning.

functions.name: toCamelCase
functions.summary:
Converts text to **camelCase** by splitting it into words, lowercasing the
first word, capitalizing the rest, then joining them back together.

Because it uses the built-in case conversion methods, the function shares
their _[locale inaccuracies](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/toLocaleLowerCase#description)_
too, making it best suited for simple strings like identifiers and internal
keys. For linguistic text processing, use [`Intl.Segmenter`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Intl/Segmenter)
with [`granularity: "word"`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Intl/Segmenter#parameters),
[`toLocaleLowerCase`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/toLocaleLowerCase),
and [`toLocaleUpperCase`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/toLocaleUpperCase)
which are purpose-built to handle nuances in languages and locales.

For other case manipulations see: [`toLowerCase`](#toLowerCase), [`toUpperCase`](#toUpperCase), [`capitalize`](#capitalize),
[`uncapitalize`](#uncapitalize), [`toKebabCase`](#toKebabCase), [`toSnakeCase`](#toSnakeCase), and [`toTitleCase`](#toTitleCase).

For *PascalCase* use `capitalize(toCamelCase(data))`.

signatures.example:
toCamelCase('hello world'); // "helloWorld"
toCamelCase('__HELLO_WORLD__'); // "helloWorld"
toCamelCase('HasHTML'); // "hasHTML"
toCamelCase('HasHTML', { preserveConsecutiveUppercase: false }); // "hasHtml"
signatures.exampleHtml: toCamelCase('hello world'); // "helloWorld" toCamelCase('__HELLO_WORLD__'); // "helloWorld" toCamelCase('HasHTML'); // "hasHTML" toCamelCase('HasHTML', { preserveConsecutiveUppercase: false }); // "hasHtml"

params.name: options
params.description:
An _optional_ object with the _optional_ property
`preserveConsecutiveUppercase` that can be used to change the way consecutive
uppercase characters are handled. Defaults to `true`.

signatures.example:
pipe('hello world', toCamelCase()); // "helloWorld"
pipe('__HELLO_WORLD__', toCamelCase()); // "helloWorld"
pipe('HasHTML', toCamelCase()); // "hasHTML"
pipe('HasHTML', toCamelCase({ preserveConsecutiveUppercase: false })); // "hasHtml"
signatures.exampleHtml: pipe('hello world', toCamelCase()); // "helloWorld" pipe('__HELLO_WORLD__', toCamelCase()); // "helloWorld" pipe('HasHTML', toCamelCase()); // "hasHTML" pipe('HasHTML', toCamelCase({ preserveConsecutiveUppercase: false })); // "hasHtml"

params.description:
An _optional_ object with the _optional_ property
`preserveConsecutiveUppercase` that can be used to change the way consecutive
uppercase characters are handled. Defaults to `true`.

functions.name: toKebabCase
functions.summary:
Converts text to **kebab-case** by splitting it into words and joining them
back together with hyphens (`-`), then lowercasing the result.

Because it uses [`toLowerCase`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/toLowerCase),
the function shares its _[locale inaccuracies](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/toLocaleLowerCase#description)_
too, making it best suited for simple strings like identifiers and internal
keys. For linguistic text processing, use [`Intl.Segmenter`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Intl/Segmenter)
with [`granularity: "word"`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Intl/Segmenter#parameters), and
[`toLocaleLowerCase`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/toLocaleLowerCase),
which are purpose-built to handle nuances in languages and locales.

For other case manipulations see: [`toLowerCase`](#toLowerCase), [`toUpperCase`](#toUpperCase), [`capitalize`](#capitalize),
[`uncapitalize`](#uncapitalize), [`toCamelCase`](#toCamelCase), [`toSnakeCase`](#toSnakeCase), and [`toTitleCase`](#toTitleCase).

For *COBOL-CASE* use `toUpperCase(toKebabCase(data))`.

signatures.exampleHtml: toKebabCase('hello world'); // "hello-world" toKebabCase('__HELLO_WORLD__'); // "hello-world"
pipe('hello world', toKebabCase()); // "hello-world" pipe('__HELLO_WORLD__', toKebabCase()); // "hello-world"

functions.name: toLowerCase
functions.summary:
Replaces all uppercase characters with their lowercase equivalents.

This function is a wrapper around the built-in
[`String.prototype.toLowerCase`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/toLowerCase)
method and shares its _[locale inaccuracies](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/toLocaleLowerCase#description)_.

For a more linguistically accurate transformation use [`toLocaleLowerCase`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/toLocaleLowerCase),
and for display purposes use CSS [`text-transform: lowercase;`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/text-transform)
which *is* locale-aware.

For other case manipulations see: [`toUpperCase`](#toUpperCase), [`capitalize`](#capitalize),
[`uncapitalize`](#uncapitalize), [`toCamelCase`](#toCamelCase), [`toKebabCase`](#toKebabCase), [`toSnakeCase`](#toSnakeCase), and
[`toTitleCase`](#toTitleCase).

signatures.exampleHtml: toLowerCase('Hello World'); // "hello world"
pipe('Hello World', toLowerCase()); // "hello world"

functions.name: toSnakeCase
functions.summary:
Converts text to **snake_case** by splitting it into words and joining them
back together with underscores (`_`), then lowercasing the result.

Because it uses [`toLowerCase`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/toLowerCase),
the function shares its _[locale inaccuracies](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/toLocaleLowerCase#description)_
too, making it best suited for simple strings like identifiers and internal
keys. For linguistic text processing, use [`Intl.Segmenter`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Intl/Segmenter)
with [`granularity: "word"`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Intl/Segmenter#parameters), and
[`toLocaleLowerCase`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/toLocaleLowerCase),
which are purpose-built to handle nuances in languages and locales.

For other case manipulations see: [`toLowerCase`](#toLowerCase), [`toUpperCase`](#toUpperCase), [`capitalize`](#capitalize),
[`uncapitalize`](#uncapitalize), [`toCamelCase`](#toCamelCase), [`toKebabCase`](#toKebabCase), and [`toTitleCase`](#toTitleCase).

For *CONSTANT_CASE* use `toUpperCase(toSnakeCase(data))`.

signatures.exampleHtml: toSnakeCase('hello world'); // "hello_world" toSnakeCase('__HELLO_WORLD__'); // "hello_world"
pipe('hello world', toSnakeCase()); // "hello_world" pipe('__HELLO_WORLD__', toSnakeCase()); // "hello_world"

functions.name: toTitleCase
functions.summary:
Converts text to **Title Case** by splitting it into words, capitalizing the
first letter of each word, then joining them back together with spaces.

Because it uses the built-in case conversion methods, the function shares
their _[locale inaccuracies](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/toLocaleLowerCase#description)_,
making it best suited for simple strings like identifiers and internal keys.
For linguistic text processing, use [`Intl.Segmenter`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Intl/Segmenter)
with [`granularity: "word"`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Intl/Segmenter#parameters),
[`toLocaleLowerCase`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/toLocaleLowerCase),
and [`toLocaleUpperCase`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/toLocaleUpperCase)
which are purpose-built to handle nuances in languages and locales.

For other case manipulations see: [`toLowerCase`](#toLowerCase), [`toUpperCase`](#toUpperCase), [`capitalize`](#capitalize),
[`uncapitalize`](#uncapitalize), [`toCamelCase`](#toCamelCase), [`toKebabCase`](#toKebabCase), and [`toSnakeCase`](#toSnakeCase).

signatures.example:
toTitleCase('hello world'); // "Hello World"
toTitleCase('--foo-bar--'); // "Foo Bar"
toTitleCase('fooBar'); // "Foo Bar"
toTitleCase('__FOO_BAR__'); // "Foo Bar"
toTitleCase('XMLHttpRequest'); // "XML Http Request"
toTitleCase('XMLHttpRequest', { preserveConsecutiveUppercase: false }); // "Xml Http Request"
signatures.exampleHtml: toTitleCase('hello world'); // "Hello World" toTitleCase('--foo-bar--'); // "Foo Bar" toTitleCase('fooBar'); // "Foo Bar" toTitleCase('__FOO_BAR__'); // "Foo Bar" toTitleCase('XMLHttpRequest'); // "XML Http Request" toTitleCase('XMLHttpRequest', { preserveConsecutiveUppercase: false }); // "Xml Http Request"

functions.name: truncate
functions.summary:
Truncates strings to a maximum length, adding an ellipsis when truncated.

Shorter strings are returned unchanged. If the omission marker is longer than
the maximum length, it will be truncated as well.

The `separator` argument provides more control by optimistically searching
for a matching cutoff point, which could be used to avoid truncating in the
middle of a word or other semantic boundary.

If you just need to limit the total length of the string, without adding an
`omission` or optimizing the cutoff point via `separator`, prefer
[`sliceString`](#sliceString) instead, which runs more efficiently.

The function counts Unicode characters, not visual graphemes, and may split
emojis, denormalized diacritics, or combining characters, in the middle. For
display purposes, prefer CSS [`text-overflow: ellipsis`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/text-overflow#ellipsis)
which is locale-aware and purpose-built for this task.

signatures.example:
truncate('Hello, world!', 8); //=> "Hello..."
truncate('cat, dog, mouse', 12, { omission: '__', separator: ',' }); //=> "cat, dog__"
signatures.exampleHtml: truncate('Hello, world!', 8); //=> "Hello..." truncate('cat, dog, mouse', 12, { omission: '__', separator: ',' }); //=> "cat, dog__"

params.description:

exceed this length.

  truncate(12, { omission: '__', separator: ',' }),
); //=> "cat, dog__"

functions.name: uncapitalize
functions.summary:
Makes the first character of a string lowercase while leaving the rest
unchanged.

It uses the built-in [`String.prototype.toLowerCase`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/toLowerCase)
for the runtime and the built-in [`Uncapitalize`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/template-literal-types.html#Uncapitalizestringtype)
utility type for typing and thus shares their _[locale inaccuracies](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/toLocaleLowerCase#description)_.

For display purposes, prefer using the CSS pseudo-element [`::first-letter`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/::first-letter) to target
just the first letter of the word, and [`text-transform: lowercase`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/text-transform#lowercase)
to lowercase it. This transformation **is** locale-aware.

For other case manipulations see: [`toUpperCase`](#toUpperCase), [`toLowerCase`](#toLowerCase), [`capitalize`](#capitalize),
[`toCamelCase`](#toCamelCase), [`toKebabCase`](#toKebabCase), [`toSnakeCase`](#toSnakeCase), and [`toTitleCase`](#toTitleCase).

signatures.exampleHtml: uncapitalize('HELLO WORLD'); // "hELLO WORLD"
pipe('HELLO WORLD', uncapitalize()); // "hELLO WORLD"

functions.name: stringToPath
functions.summary:
A utility to allow JSONPath-like strings to be used in other utilities which
take an array of path segments as input (e.g. [`prop`](#prop), [`setPath`](#setPath), etc...).
The main purpose of this utility is to act as a bridge between the runtime
implementation that converts the path to an array, and the type-system that
parses the path string **type** into an array **type**. This type allows us
to return fine-grained types and to enforce correctness at the type-level.

We **discourage** using this utility for new code. This utility is for legacy
code that already contains path strings (which are accepted by Lodash). We
strongly recommend using *path arrays* instead as they provide better
developer experience via significantly faster type-checking, fine-grained
error messages, and automatic typeahead suggestions for each segment of the
path.

There are a bunch of limitations to this utility derived from the
limitations of the type itself, these are usually edge-cases around deeply
nested paths, escaping, whitespaces, and empty segments. This is true even
in cases where the runtime implementation can better handle them, this is
intentional. See the tests for this utility for more details and the
expected outputs*.

signatures.exampleHtml: stringToPath('a.b[0].c'); // => ['a', 'b', 0, 'c']

signatures.signatureHtml: type DeepPartial<T> = T extends object ? { [P in keyof T]?: DeepPartial<T[P]> } : T;

functions.name: defaultTo
functions.summary:
A stricter wrapper around the [Nullish coalescing operator `??`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Nullish_coalescing_operator)
that ensures that the fallback matches the type of the data. Only works
when data can be `null` or `undefined`.

Notice that `Number.NaN` is not nullish and would not result in returning the
fallback!

signatures.example:
defaultTo('hello' as string | undefined, 'world'); //=> "hello"
defaultTo(undefined as string | undefined, 'world'); //=> "world"

functions.name: tap
functions.summary:
Calls the given function with the given value, then returns the given value.
The return value of the provided function is ignored.

This allows "tapping into" a function sequence in a pipe, to perform side
effects on intermediate results.

signatures.exampleHtml: tap('foo', console.log); // => "foo"

params.name: value
params.description: The value to pass into the function.

signatures.example:
pipe(
  [-5, -1, 2, 3],
  filter((n) => n > 0),
  tap(console.log), // prints [2, 3]
  map((n) => n * 2),
); // => [4, 6]
